content:
Philip Ruddock, a former Liberal minister, has been appointed to assess if Australian law sufficiently safeguards the right to religious freedom. This inquiry, set by the cabinet and announced on a Wednesday, aims to preempt a contentious discussion on religious amendments within the same-sex marriage legislation. Treasurer Scott Morrison, however, emphasized that this review should not replace the need for those amendments.

***
Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull commented on the importance of scrutinizing religious freedom, especially in the context of the affirmative vote on marriage equality and the forthcoming related legislation. Although some senior conservatives like Peter Dutton and Mathias Cormann have suggested that a bill focused solely on religious freedom could be debated next year, others, including Morrison and Liberal senator David Fawcett, believe it should concurrently be addressed with the marriage bill.

***
Ruddock is tasked with reporting his findings by March 31. Turnbull highlighted that numerous proposals to alter legislation to protect religious freedoms have been proposed recently; however, many extend beyond the scope of marriage issues. He stressed that Parliament should approach these cautiously to avoid any unintended legal repercussions. 

***
The government is wary of creating potential uncertainties through broadly framed bills of rights-style declarations. Turnbull described the effort as a “timely expert stocktake” needed to guide the consideration of any essential legal changes. He reiterated the complexity involved in legislating core freedoms like those concerning religion.

***
Turnbull praised Ruddock as the ideal candidate for leading this review, citing his experience as Australia’s special envoy for human rights. This background presumably equips him with the nuanced understanding required to evaluate the intricate balance between legislative action and the protection of religious freedoms in Australia.
